title: Everyday astronomy and stargazing
subtitle: A night-sky trip note, setting up a telescope, views on stargazing, backyard skywatching, and a local astronomy club

parts.title: Sentence comprehension: Stargazing trip note
parts.instructions: Read the short email from a friend. Choose the best word for each gap (1-5).
parts.passage:
Hi Hugo,

I just got back from the weekend stargazing trip on the coast, and the sky was amazing. Although the weather forecast had warned us about heavy clouds, the wind blew them [1] just before midnight. Our group leader, Sonia, had reminded everyone to [2] warm layers and a red-light torch so our eyes could adjust to the dark. We spotted Jupiter and its bright moons through her telescope, [3] was the first time I had ever seen another planet so clearly. I even managed to take a sharp photo of the Milky Way, [4] though I only used a basic tripod. Let me know if you are free next Saturday to come [5] on our next evening walk!

Best,
Freya

questions.explanation: 'Blew them away' is the phrasal verb meaning the wind cleared the clouds from the sky.
'Wear warm layers' is the natural verb + noun combination here; 'dress' does not take clothes as a direct object, and 'put' needs 'on'.
'Which' introduces a non-defining relative clause after a comma referring back to the whole event.
'Even though' is a conjunction meaning 'despite the fact that'; 'despite' and 'although' cannot precede 'though'.
'Come along' means to join someone on an activity or trip.

parts.title: Text cohesion: First night with binoculars
parts.instructions: The first sentence of the text is in the right place. Put the five sentences (A-E) into the correct order (gaps 1-5) to make a clear story.
parts.passage: Last Friday evening, I carried a pair of ordinary binoculars and a folding chair into my back garden to try stargazing for the first time. [1] [2] [3] [4] [5]
sentences: Once my eyes had grown used to the darkness, I pointed the binoculars towards the bright half-moon rising above the trees.
To help with that problem, I rested my elbows firmly on the wooden arms of my chair until the picture became completely still.
First, I switched off the kitchen lamp behind me so no indoor light would reflect off the glass lenses.
Seeing those tiny craters and shadows across the moon's surface made me feel as if I were floating above another world.
At first the image shook slightly in my hands, making it hard to focus on the silver edge.

gaps.explanation: 'First, I switched off the kitchen lamp behind me' starts the preparation right after walking into the garden.
'Once my eyes had grown used to the darkness' follows turning off the light and introduces looking at the half-moon.
'At first the image shook slightly in my hands' describes the initial difficulty when looking at the moon.
'To help with that problem' refers directly to the shaking image in the previous sentence and explains how to steady the binoculars.
'Seeing those tiny craters and shadows' follows once the picture became still and closes the experience.

parts.title: Opinion matching: Watching the night sky
parts.instructions: Four people (A-D) give their opinions about amateur astronomy and stargazing. Match each statement (1-7) to the correct person. You can use each person more than once.

texts.title: Freya
texts.text: People often think you need to spend hundreds of pounds on a large telescope before you can enjoy astronomy. In my experience, beginners actually learn the sky much faster with just a printed star map and their own eyes. Heavy equipment takes twenty minutes to carry outside and set up, so you end up staying indoors on cold evenings. A light pair of binoculars lets you step out for ten minutes whenever the clouds clear.

texts.title: Hugo
texts.text: I live near the middle of a busy city, where orange streetlamps hide all but the brightest stars. Because of that light pollution, I usually drive forty minutes into the hills on clear weekends to see the Milky Way properly. It is frustrating to spend petrol and time travelling, so I joined a local campaign asking the council to fit downward-facing covers on new streetlamps.

texts.title: Sonia
texts.text: I used to stare at sky apps on my phone while standing in the garden, yet the bright screen kept spoiling my night vision. Now I leave my phone in my pocket and sketch the shape of the moon and nearby stars in a paper notebook with a pencil. Drawing slowly forces me to notice small details I would normally miss, even if my sketches never look like professional photographs.

texts.title: Ibrahim
texts.text: For me, the real joy of stargazing is sharing it with neighbours who have never looked through a lens before. Twice a month, I set up my telescope on the park path and invite families walking past to look at Saturn's rings. Watching a child's face light up when they realise that bright dot in the sky is an actual planet never gets old.

parts.title: Long text comprehension: Backyard astronomy
parts.instructions: Read the article about how everyday people study the night sky. Match each paragraph (1-7) to the best heading (A-H). There is one extra heading that you do not need.

paragraphs.text: For thousands of years, watching the stars was part of ordinary life rather than a specialist science. Farmers checked seasonal star patterns to decide when to plant crops, while sailors used bright northern stars to steer wooden boats safely across open water. Because there were no electric streetlamps, every village enjoyed a dark canopy overhead every clear night. Families sitting outside after sunset knew the names of major star groups just as well as they knew local hills and rivers.

During the twentieth century, rapid growth in cities and roads changed how people saw the night sky. Bright outdoor signs, office windows, and orange highway lights sent wasted light upward into the air, creating an orange glow above most towns. Today, more than half of the world's population lives under skies too bright to show the Milky Way. Many children grow up seeing only the moon and a handful of the brightest planets.

Even under city lights, however, beginner skywatchers can still spot plenty of interesting sights from a balcony or small garden. The moon looks dramatic through simple binoculars because shadows along its edge make craters stand out clearly. Bright planets such as Venus, Jupiter, and Mars easily shine through city haze, and their slow movement from week to week against the background stars is easy to follow without expensive gear.

Modern smartphones have also changed how newcomers find their way around the heavens. Free star-chart apps use a phone's compass so that pointing the screen upward instantly labels whatever star or planet sits in front of you. While experienced observers warn against staring at bright screens for too long, most apps now include a red-light mode that protects night vision while helping beginners locate unfamiliar star patterns.

Amateur astronomers do far more than simply admire pretty views; many contribute useful measurements to professional researchers. Backyard volunteers regularly time when distant stars briefly dim as an asteroid passes in front of them, or report sudden bright spots on Jupiter's clouds. Because professional observatories have tight schedules and cannot watch every corner of the sky at once, thousands of patient hobbyists provide an essential extra pair of eyes.

To protect the remaining dark areas of the countryside, many rural parks and islands have applied to become official dark-sky reserves. Local councils in these regions replace upward-pointing floodlights with warm, shielded lamps that shine only onto paths and roads where people actually walk. As a result, visitors travel to these quiet villages especially for night-sky holidays, bringing welcome income to small guesthouses and cafés during winter months.

If you feel curious about starting this hobby yourself, the best first step costs nothing at all. Wrap up warmly, wait twenty minutes away from bright windows so your eyes adjust, and learn three or four easy shapes such as the Big Dipper or Orion. Joining a local astronomy club is another great move, since friendly members are usually happy to let newcomers look through several types of telescopes before buying anything.

What you can still see from a bright town

gaps.explanation: Paragraph 1 describes how farmers, sailors, and villagers used the night sky in everyday life long before electric lighting.
Paragraph 2 explains how city expansion and outdoor streetlamps created light pollution that hides the Milky Way.
Paragraph 3 points out that the moon and bright planets can still be observed clearly from urban gardens and balconies.
Paragraph 4 discusses how smartphone star-chart apps and red-light modes help beginners identify stars and planets.
Paragraph 5 explains how amateur volunteers record timings and cloud changes that professional observatories cannot monitor alone.
Paragraph 6 shows how shielded lamps create dark-sky reserves that attract winter visitors to rural guesthouses and cafés.
Paragraph 7 gives simple advice for beginners: dress warmly, let your eyes adjust, and try a local club before buying gear.

parts.title: Monologue comprehension
parts.instructions: Listen to two speakers giving short talks: first an astronomy teacher about running school sky nights (questions 1-2), then a dark-sky park ranger about reducing light pollution (questions 3-4). Choose the best answer for each question.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: First, you will hear Freya, a science teacher, talking about organising evening stargazing events for school students.

turns.speaker: freya
turns.text: When I first suggested holding winter stargazing evenings on our school playing field, colleagues warned me that teenagers would get bored standing outside in the cold. To be honest, the weather is still our biggest headache — twice this term we had to cancel at short notice because thick clouds rolled in. Yet whenever the sky stays clear, the students are completely amazed. What really surprised me wasn't their excitement over seeing the moon through a telescope; it was how many quiet students who rarely speak in daytime science lessons started asking thoughtful questions about distance and time. If any teacher wants to try a similar event, my main tip is to invite parents to bring hot drinks and keep the session under an hour so nobody gets too cold.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Now you will hear Ross, a park ranger, talking about protecting dark skies in a national park.

turns.speaker: ross
turns.text: People often think creating a dark-sky park means turning off every single streetlamp and leaving villages in total darkness. In fact, our goal isn't darkness for its own sake — it's simply pointing lights downward where people walk instead of wasting electricity shining into the clouds. Over the past three years, we worked with local shop owners to fit simple metal covers over bright outdoor signs. At first, a few café owners worried that dimmer streets might put off evening customers. Actually, the opposite happened: winter weekend bookings rose because visitors now drive here especially to see the Milky Way. Looking ahead, we hope to train twenty local teenagers as sky guides so they can lead summer walks for tourists.

questions.explanation: Freya says the weather is their biggest headache, forcing them to cancel twice when thick clouds rolled in.

questions.prompt: What surprised Freya most about the students during the evening sessions?
questions.explanation: Freya was surprised by how many quiet students who rarely speak in daytime lessons asked thoughtful questions.

questions.prompt: According to Ross, what is the main goal of a dark-sky park?
